body:
Why thorium is central to India's long-term plan

The third stage of India's nuclear programme is intended to use India's large thorium resource potential for sustained nuclear electricity generation. Its central concept is the conversion of thorium-232 into uranium-233.

Thorium-232 is a fertile material. It does not by itself provide the fissile material needed to maintain the intended nuclear chain reaction. However, after absorbing a neutron and undergoing subsequent nuclear transformations, thorium-232 can produce uranium-233, which is fissile.

Thorium fuel cycle: A nuclear fuel cycle in which fertile thorium-232 is converted into fissile uranium-233, and the uranium-233 is subsequently used to release energy through fission.

A thorium-based reactor system therefore needs an initial source of fissile material, such as uranium-233 or another suitable fissile material. It cannot simply begin producing power from thorium-232 alone.

How the 3 stages connect

The first 2 stages establish the fissile resources needed for wider thorium use. The sequence is important:

  1. Natural uranium containing uranium-235 is used in first-stage PHWRs. Some uranium-238 is converted into plutonium-239.
  2. Plutonium recovered from spent PHWR fuel is used in second-stage fast breeder reactors. These reactors are intended to expand the available fissile-material inventory.
  3. Breeder systems can support the conversion of thorium-232 into uranium-233. The resulting uranium-233 is intended to provide fuel for third-stage thorium-based systems.

The long-term strategy requires an adequate fissile-material base before thorium can be used on a large scale. This explains why thorium resources do not automatically translate into immediate commercial thorium electricity generation.

Advanced Heavy Water Reactor and research applications

The Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) is an Indian reactor concept developed to support the use of thorium-based fuel. It represents a proposed route for demonstrating technologies needed for larger-scale thorium utilisation. It should not be treated as an established fleet of commercial third-stage power stations.

India has already carried out experimental work involving thorium. Thorium-based fuel has been irradiated in research reactors, and uranium-233 has been recovered from irradiated thorium material.

The KAMINI research reactor at Kalpakkam has used uranium-233 obtained through such work. KAMINI demonstrates an important research application of uranium-233, but it is not a commercial third-stage nuclear power station.

Development status: In its 23 July 2026 parliamentary statement, the Department of Atomic Energy described large-scale thorium utilisation as a future step, dependent on adequate fast breeder reactor capacity and continuing research. For the content cutoff of 15 November 2026, the third stage should therefore be understood as a long-term development objective, not as a commercially deployed national stage.

What is a closed nuclear fuel cycle?

A nuclear fuel cycle includes the main activities associated with obtaining fuel materials, preparing nuclear fuel, using it in a reactor and managing the fuel after irradiation.

In an open or once-through fuel cycle, spent fuel is managed without recovering and reusing its uranium and plutonium through reprocessing. In a closed fuel cycle, useful nuclear materials are recovered from spent fuel and can be fabricated into new fuel.

India's three-stage strategy depends on the closed fuel cycle because the material produced in one stage helps supply the next. Plutonium recovered after Stage 1 is used in Stage 2, while breeding and further fuel-cycle development support the eventual use of uranium-233 in Stage 3.

Closed does not mean waste-free

Reprocessing does not eliminate radioactive waste. Fission products and other radioactive residues still require separation, treatment and safe management. The word closed refers to the recovery and reuse of useful nuclear materials, not to the complete disappearance of waste.

The principal advantage of this approach is that it can extract more useful energy from available uranium and, in the longer term, permit the utilisation of thorium that cannot serve as a direct replacement for fissile uranium fuel.

Prelims focus

  • Thorium-232 is fertile; uranium-233 produced from it is fissile.
  • Stage 3 envisages large-scale use of uranium-233 derived from thorium.
  • AHWR stands for Advanced Heavy Water Reactor.
  • KAMINI is a research reactor at Kalpakkam associated with the use of uranium-233.
  • India's three-stage programme is based on a closed fuel cycle.
  • Trap: A closed fuel cycle involves recovery and reuse of useful materials; it does not eliminate radioactive waste.

[Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, About Us, section Atomic Energy in India, consulted 15 November 2026; Department of Atomic Energy, Parliamentary Question: Nuclear Fuel Programme, 23 July 2026; Department of Atomic Energy, Parliamentary Question: Nuclear Power Programme, 23 July 2026; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, chapter Mineral and Energy Resources, printed pp. 80–82.]

Open fuel cycles manage spent fuel without reuse; closed cycles recover uranium and plutonium for new fuel while managing radioactive waste separately.

title: Stage 3: Thorium, Uranium-233 and the Closed Nuclear Fuel Cycle

body:
Locate the 4 stations on India's map

A nuclear power station's location and its reactor technology are separate facts. For prelims, both must be known. The 4 stations covered here are located in Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

Kakrapar is in southern Gujarat, near the Tapi River. Tarapur is on the western coast of Maharashtra, north of Mumbai. Kaiga is in the Uttara Kannada region of Karnataka, near the Western Ghats. Kudankulam is on the southern coast of Tamil Nadu in Tirunelveli district.

These positions help distinguish similarly named stations. In particular, Kaiga is in Karnataka, while Kakrapar is in Gujarat.

Match each station with its reactor type

India operates different types of nuclear reactors. The presence of PHWRs in the first stage of its indigenous programme does not mean every nuclear power station in the country is a PHWR.

Power stationStateExisting unit types and capacities
Kaiga Generating Station (KGS)Karnataka4 PHWR units of 220 MWe each; total 880 MWe
Kakrapar Atomic Power Station (KAPS)Gujarat2 PHWR units of 220 MWe and 2 PHWR units of 700 MWe; total 1,840 MWe
Kudankulam Nuclear Power Station (KKNPS)Tamil Nadu2 PWR units of VVER-1000 type, 1,000 MWe each; total 2,000 MWe
Tarapur Atomic Power Station (TAPS)Maharashtra2 BWR units of 160 MWe and 2 PHWR units of 540 MWe; total 1,400 MWe

These figures describe the existing reactor units and their rated electrical capacities, not the amount of electricity being generated at a particular moment. Individual units may be shut down for maintenance or other reasons.

Kaiga and Kakrapar: PHWR stations

Kaiga Generating Station has 4 existing 220 MWe PHWR units. It is situated in Karnataka's Uttara Kannada district. Its association with PHWR technology makes it an example of the reactor type central to the first stage.

Kakrapar Atomic Power Station is located near Anumala and Vyara in Tapi district, Gujarat. It stands in the Tapi River region of southern Gujarat. Its 4 existing units are PHWRs: the older KAPS-1 and KAPS-2 units are rated at 220 MWe each, while KAPS-3 and KAPS-4 are rated at 700 MWe each.

The newer Kakrapar units have particular importance in India's indigenous PHWR development. According to NPCIL's operating records, KAPS-3 began commercial operation on 30 June 2023 and KAPS-4 on 31 March 2024.

Gujarat connection: Kakrapar is the nuclear power station associated with Gujarat. Its existing 220 MWe and 700 MWe units are all PHWRs. Do not confuse the nuclear power station with the nearby Kakrapar dam and its water-related infrastructure.

Kudankulam: VVER-type pressurised water reactors

Kudankulam Nuclear Power Station is in Tamil Nadu. Its existing KKNPS-1 and KKNPS-2 units are VVER-1000 reactors, a type of Pressurised Water Reactor (PWR) developed using Russian technology.

VVER reactors use ordinary light water as moderator and coolant. They are therefore different from the heavy-water PHWRs associated with India's first-stage strategy.

Each of the 2 existing Kudankulam units has a rated electrical capacity of 1,000 MWe. Their commercial operation dates are 31 December 2014 for Unit 1 and 31 March 2017 for Unit 2.

Tarapur: both BWR and PHWR technologies

Tarapur Atomic Power Station in Maharashtra is particularly important because it has more than one reactor type.

Its first 2 units, TAPS-1 and TAPS-2, are Boiling Water Reactors (BWRs) rated at 160 MWe each. They began commercial operation on 28 October 1969, making Tarapur the site of India's first commercial nuclear power station.

The later TAPS-3 and TAPS-4 units are PHWRs rated at 540 MWe each. Therefore, the statement that Tarapur consists entirely of PHWRs is incorrect.

A BWR uses ordinary light water, which boils in the reactor to produce steam. This differs from a PHWR, which uses heavy water as moderator and primary coolant. The elementary distinction is sufficient for identifying the reactor type in a location-based prelims question.

Existing stations and new projects must be distinguished

Reactor construction is an ongoing process, so the number of planned units at a location may be greater than the number already in commercial operation.

In its 29 July 2026 parliamentary update, the Department of Atomic Energy listed Kaiga-5 and Kaiga-6, each planned at 700 MWe, and Kudankulam-3 to Kudankulam-6, each planned at 1,000 MWe, among projects under construction or commissioning. These planned additional units must not be counted as already operating in the existing-unit totals above.

The station classifications and existing-unit capacities in this lesson follow NPCIL's reactor records and its reported operating data for April–August 2026. The construction-status statements follow the Department of Atomic Energy's update of 29 July 2026. These are the specified evidence periods for the lesson cutoff of 15 November 2026.

Connect the plant map to the three-stage programme

The 4 locations illustrate an important distinction between India's long-term nuclear fuel strategy and its actual fleet of power reactors.

  • Kaiga and Kakrapar: PHWR stations using the reactor technology associated with Stage 1.
  • Tarapur: A combination of older BWR units and later PHWR units.
  • Kudankulam: PWR units of the VVER type, not PHWRs.

The second-stage PFBR is located separately at Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu. It should not be confused with Kudankulam or with the PHWR units of the Madras Atomic Power Station, which are also at Kalpakkam. The third stage remains a longer-term thorium-based programme rather than a group of established commercial thorium stations on this map.

Prelims focus

  • Kaiga is in Karnataka and has 4 existing 220 MWe PHWR units.
  • Kakrapar is in Gujarat and has 2 existing 220 MWe PHWR units and 2 existing 700 MWe PHWR units.
  • Kudankulam is in Tamil Nadu and its existing units are VVER-type PWRs.
  • Tarapur is in Maharashtra and has both BWR and PHWR units.
  • Tarapur's first commercial nuclear power units began operation in 1969.
  • PFBR is at Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu, not at Kudankulam.
  • Trap: A station's planned expansion units are not necessarily already in commercial operation.

[NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, chapter Mineral and Energy Resources, printed p. 82; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter Mineral and Power Resources, printed pp. 34–35, 2018–19 printing; Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited, Reactors in Operation, consulted 15 November 2026; Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited, Operating Performance: Kakrapar and Kudankulam, April–August 2026 reporting period, consulted 15 November 2026; Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited, Annual Report 2024–25, Our Plants, Projects and Locations, p. 372, and Our Presence map, p. 373; Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited, Right to Information, station contact locations, consulted 15 November 2026; Department of Atomic Energy, Parliamentary Question: Operational Performance of NPCIL Nuclear Power Plants, 29 July 2026.]
title: India's Nuclear Power Plant Map: Kaiga, Kakrapar, Kudankulam and Tarapur
